Big Question
Today’s Wonder

You learn the spaceship the way Ransom does, one wrong guess at a time. Why would a writer make you share his mistakes?

🎯
Objectives
By the end of this lesson…
📖Reading: I will read Chapters 3 and 4, from Ransom waking in a hot, dark room to Weston leaving the breakfast room.
🔭Craft: I will tell point of view (where the narrator stands) from perspective (a character’s attitude), and show how Lewis builds a strange place out of Ransom’s mistakes.
🔤Words: I will learn five words: lassitude, portentous, infringe, alacrity, and magnanimous.

🛰️ Where Is the Ship?
Place it on the line, then say what Ransom is looking at

Weston gives the ship’s position in one sentence: “Standing out from Earth about eighty-five thousand miles.” Place the ship there. Drag it along the line, or tap the spot, then lock it in.

miles from Earth (distances to scale, planet sizes not)
Earth
Moon
239,000
ship
Drag the ship, or tap the line.
The full Moon from homeabout half a degree wide
The Earth from the shipabout five degrees wide

The Earth is 7,918 miles across. From 85,000 miles out, it looks about ten times as wide as the full Moon does from home. Both discs are drawn to the same scale. Lewis makes it bigger still: “filling almost half the sky.” A novelist may stretch what a measurement would show.

So what is in Ransom’s skylight?

Ulysses
Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1842) · Lines 18–32 of 70
I am a part of all that I have met; Yet all experience is an arch wherethro’ Gleams that untravell’d world, whose margin fades For ever and for ever when I move. How dull it is to pause, to make an end, To rust unburnish’d, not to shine in use! As tho’ to breathe were life. Life piled on life Were all too little, and of one to me Little remains: but every hour is saved From that eternal silence, something more, A bringer of new things; and vile it were For some three suns to store and hoard myself, And this gray spirit yearning in desire To follow knowledge, like a sinking star, Beyond the utmost bound of human thought.
wherethro’: through which · margin: edge · unburnish’d: unpolished · three suns: three years · yearning: longing

🔤 Words: Heat, Light, and Rights
Five more of this week’s ten words. Learn them before you read.

Say the meaning first, then tap the card to check.

😴
lassitude
tap to flip and hear it
lassitude
A heavy, tired weakness. Ransom wakes with a headache and a general lassitude.
🌑
portentous
tap to flip and hear it
portentous
Ominous: seeming to warn that something huge is coming. Ransom sits and stares at the portentous moon.
🚧
infringe
tap to flip and hear it
infringe
To break into or violate, as a right. Weston admits they have had to infringe Ransom’s rights.
⚡
alacrity
tap to flip and hear it
alacrity
Cheerful, quick eagerness. The ship’s dry heat gives Ransom not drowsiness but intense alacrity.
🤲
magnanimous
tap to flip and hear it
magnanimous
Generous of spirit; big-hearted. At breakfast Ransom feels vigilant, courageous, and magnanimous, as he has seldom felt on Earth.

🎓 Questions from Professor Lovelore
She asks. You answer.
0 / 3
Professor Lovelore
First question. Asked how he knows the name Malacandra, Weston answers only, “From the inhabitants.” What does that tell you about this trip?
Your answer
Professor Lovelore
Next. Ransom asks how the ship works, and Weston says they work by “exploiting the less observed properties of solar radiation.” What is that answer really doing?
Your answer
Professor Lovelore
Last question. When Weston walks in, “No reproach, no demand for an explanation,” rises to Ransom’s lips. Why not?
Your answer
Professor Lovelore

Well done. Look at what those three moments share. Each one reaches you from beside Ransom: the narrator tells the story in the third person, stays close to him, and mostly lets you learn things when he does.

That is point of view. How Ransom regards Weston, and what he refuses to accept from him, is his perspective. Because we stand so close to him, we share his mistakes, and that is how the ship comes to feel real.

You have seen the ship through Ransom’s eyes. Now sort what he thought from what was true.
